title: Rare clinical entity of cystic meningioma in an elderly patient: A case report and review of the literature
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
case_prompt:
A 64-year-old right-handed woman presented with a 3-week history of progressive speech difficulty, initially mild and insidious but evolving to an inability to name objects or family members. She also reported unilateral fronto-temporal headaches, worse in the early morning and occasionally at night, gait unsteadiness, and episodes of urinary incontinence. There was no vomiting, seizures, visual disturbance, or other focal neurologic deficits. Her medical, surgical, family, and medication histories were unremarkable. 

On examination, she was alert and oriented but had anomic aphasia and agraphia. Pupils were equal and reactive. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were normal. On the right, there was hyperreflexia in both upper and lower extremities, a positive pronator drift, and motor strength of 4/5. The left side was normal.

Brain imaging with contrast-enhanced CT and MRI revealed a 4×4×4 cm extra-axial cystic lesion in the left fronto-temporal region. On MRI it was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, surrounded by vasogenic edema, and causing a midline shift.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neuroblastoma was considered because cystic extra-axial masses can mimic neuroblastoma in appearance — “It is often misinterpreted as a neuroblastoma, metastasis, hemangioblastoma, or glial tumor.”  
2. Metastatic tumor was considered given the cystic brain lesion but imaging showed meningeal interaction and contrast enhancement typical of meningioma — “The sole findings that pointed to a meningioma were the mass's interaction with the meninges and the stark contrast enhancement.”  
3. Hemangioblastoma was considered due to the vascular and cystic appearance; however, the presence of a CSF or vascular cleft and white matter buckling indicated an extra-axial origin — “The presence of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or a vascular gap between the meningioma and normal parenchyma, white matter buckling, and cortical thinning are imaging characteristics of an extra-axial meningioma.”  
4. Glial tumor (glioma) was considered but MRI demonstrated classic extra-axial findings, including a dural tail, which are not features of intra-axial gliomas — “MRI revealed all the signs of a meningioma, including a dural tail, a CSF fissure, and buckled white matter.”
